So how's the collaboration that you've been doing with the Northeast Public

55 Health? How is that working for us, and is that giving us some leverage knowing that we don't have WHO?

That’s a great question. That’s a great question. And so, the collaborative has been a wonderful, wonderful place to share best practices, to share information, to plan and coordinate, and to really establish a response that meets the moment. To me, it's a war on science, and we cannot afford that. And, and the thing about vaccine, when you're associate it with autism, knowing there's a big increase in autism, especially in the Black and Brown community, that's already lack of trust, I find it very irresponsible.

56 And I'm— it's very alarming to me for the federal level to take that stand.

Yeah, what we're hearing from the federal government is absolutely leading to confusion and giving people, quite frankly, inaccurate, false information. And so we can't complain about it. We have to act. And, you know, what we are doing in the city is we are acting. We are not waiting for the federal government to come and tell us what we're going to do for New Yorkers or what the information should be that we will share with New Yorkers. We are relying on— look, this department has some of the best public health experts, not just in the country, in the world.
I know we do.
You know, and so, you know, we're leaning on that expertise to lead.

And I know my time is up. The last one I'm going to say, the concern of the cut on federal funding and having this and how we're going to make sure that people get the information, the real information, not the fake information. So thank you, Chair, appreciate your time.

Absolutely. Council Member Feliz?

Thank you. Thank you so much, Chair, for this important hearing. Thank you for working on the many issues that we're discussing today, including vaccines and also transparency related to meals and drinks that New Yorkers consume. And I also want to thank you, the Department of Health, for being here and also for the many conversations that we've had offline about these topics. I'm proud to be working on two bills being heard today, Introduction 196 and Introduction 547, which will help educate New Yorkers on what they consume and specifically educate New Yorkers on the levels of sodium and sugar in their meals. As we know, the effects of overconsumption of sodium are detrimental and well-documented. It continues to be a top cause of health complications, including high blood pressure, heart failure, and much more. This is literally a silent killer and it's especially a silent killer in some of our most vulnerable communities. And speaking about the dangers of sodium, there are restaurants that have extreme and disturbing levels of sodium in meals, disturbing

58 levels that are not even properly disclosed. Little Caesars, for example, has a pizza pie containing 11,000— approximately 11,000 milligrams of sodium. If you eat that pizza pie in one meal, you'll be consuming five times what you should have in an entire day. That is beyond concerning. And even worse, these are levels of sodium that are not even properly disclosed to customers. And even much worse, there's a Little Caesars located in almost every single corner of communities that are already suffering from health complications. Restaurants like these are literally killing people in our community, people who don't realize how much sodium they're consuming. Now, as all of you know and mentioned, we do have some rules related to transparency. We require basically a salt shaker icon when there's— when the rule is triggered, when there's a high sodium meal. But why speak to residents with coded or technical language? Those who don't understand what the icon means, are they supposed to just Google it? And also, who goes to different places and just starts Googling and trying to understand every single icon when there's billions of notices and warnings everywhere you go? That's not effective. Having a

59 warning that people don't understand has the same effect as having no warning at all. So it's crucial that we speak to New Yorkers in plain language so that warnings and information that we're providing can actually be understood, which should be, of course, our goal. So my bill will require many things, including high sodium and high sugar be written in red capital bold letters for meals that trigger the rule. Wouldn't be the first to have such rule. Philadelphia has actually a nearly identical rule. They require the icon but also red, white, bold letters for high sodium meals. And of course, this rule is not at all to tell New Yorkers what they should consume or what they shouldn't consume. New Yorkers are obviously free to consume whatever they want or will. But this rule, it would be a rule to provide New Yorkers with basic information about what they're consuming so that they don't make decisions that are detrimental to their health. So that is my opening statement. I'll briefly, ask some questions. So in the bill you mentioned– and again, thank you for the many conversations that we've had on this bill. So in the— in your testimony, you mentioned that you're not fully there with supporting the bill,

60 but that you look forward to having conversations. The bill requires a few things. Number one, that high sodium or high sugar be written in red capital bold letters. Also, it'll bring down the level that would trigger the rule to 1,800, and then it'll require some disclosures about the effects of sodium. Which are the parts that you disagree with, and are there any of those parts that you might could get on board with?

Yeah, first of all, thank you, Councilmember Feliz, for your leadership on this issue. I'm going to take them one by one. So first– and I'm going to pass it over to my colleague to share a little bit more. First, on the sodium bill, you know, we know that high levels of sodium are killing New Yorkers, absolutely. And we know that this department has been a leader on this issue in this city in the past. You know, at the end of the day, our goals are completely aligned on this, and, you know, what really is at stake is deciding what the details are around this. I think I'll pass it over to my colleague to speak a little more there.

And I’m sorry, also have a few questions. If we could be a little bit concise with

61 the answers. I know our chair is pretty tough with the time, so trying to get a few questions in. Thank you.

Absolutely. Good morning, Council Member Feliz. I'll be as quick as I can. So to jump right into it, we do have some concerns around equitable access to a red icon, particularly with New Yorkers that have impaired vision or low vision. Red is a little bit more difficult to see, and we do, to your point, want to make sure that as many New Yorkers as possible have access to this clear, transparent information to help support eating, healthy eating, in our chain restaurants.

Okay. Which of the three parts, though, do you have the biggest issues with, and are there any parts that you would be willing to get on board with? So for example, would you be willing to get on board with a rule that is— could be complied with in a heartbeat, right? Just requiring high sodium or high sugar in red, white, bold letters for rules that trigger the rule.

Yeah.

Would you be willing to get on board with that part at least? Yeah. What I can say, council member, is that warning labels only work if people can see them. And, you know, our, you know, initial choice of color wasn't done by happenstance. You know, we chose that to, you know, ensure that folks who have, for instance, red-green color blindness can see. And so in this case, I think that there is an opportunity to continue the conversation and get to the same place on exactly what the warnings will look like. But pass it over to my colleague to see if she has anything else to add.

And I'd just like to thank you again for raising some of these very serious concerns about some of the food that we can access in our chain restaurants. One more question, but I'm also gonna ask that you continue to meet with the council member around this legislation. Is that fair?

Good day, Chair Schulman and members of the Health Committee. I am Cassandra Stuart, lead budget and policy policy analyst on health at the New York City Independent Budget Office, IBO. I appreciate the opportunity to discuss access to childhood vaccines in New York City with you today. On Monday, March 2nd, IBO published a report on how federal changes to vaccine policies could impact New York City, providing broader context on the occurrence of reportable infectious diseases, both generally and specifically in children across the city. I've brought copies for the committee today along with a longer version of this testimony, which is also available on IBO's website. This report is

84 the latest in a series that examines areas of New York City's budget, economy, and operations that are particularly reliant on federal funding, subject to notable federal policy changes, or both. These reports are intended to inform public discussion by objectively highlighting how federal decisions may affect the city. Critical highlights of the report include the following. As far as federal and state policy context, in December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, CDC, modified its guidance for hepatitis B vaccinations so that the vaccine will now only be administered to babies born to women who test negative for the virus and after consultation between parents and clinicians. A birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine was first recommended for all newborns in 1991. Since then, infections in children and teens have declined by 99 percent. Hepatitis B is a serious, potentially fatal liver infection. In January 2026, The pediatric vaccination schedule was further modified. Six additional vaccines— those for hepatitis A, meningococcal disease, rotavirus, respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, influenza, and COVID-19— were shifted from being recommended for all children to being recommended

85 only for high-risk and/or– high-risk groups and/or for those who consult with a healthcare provider. For the purpose of this testimony, these six conditions and hepatitis B will be collectively referred to as diseases of interest. The New York State Department of Health stated that its current childhood vaccination policies will remain the same despite the announced changes at the federal level. Further, during the State of the State address, Governor Kathy Hochul announced plans to advance legislation that will ensure New York has the ability to set its own immunization standards for school eligibility, clinical practice, and insurance coverage. While current federal changes to the childhood vaccination schedule do not necessarily equate to funding cuts, they set a precedent for future changes. Modifications to the populations for which vaccines are recommended, or to the vaccines that are recommended, may redefine how officials promote the safety of the general public from infectious and potentially fatal diseases. The Federal Vaccines for Children program, VFC, provides vaccines through enrolled public and private healthcare providers at no cost to patients, including through NYC Health's

86 own immunization clinics. VFC provides vaccines to children who are uninsured, Medicaid eligible or enrolled, American Indian or Alaska Native, or underinsured. As for the New York City landscape, in the city, over 60 percent of children are eligible for vaccines through VFC, and there are more than 1,000 providers enrolled in the VFC program. In evaluating the spread of cases of diseases of interest across age groups, IBO found that in 2023, children from birth through age 14 sometimes accounted for more than 50 percent of cases of the diseases of interest, 53 percent of rotavirus cases, and 64 percent of RSV cases. There is some overlap between the diseases of interest and vaccine requirements for attendance in New York City schools. Specifically, hepatitis B, influenza, and meningococcal conjugate ACWY vaccinations are required at various points through to grade 12. In closing, while federal vaccine guidance on the pediatric vaccination schedule has shifted several vaccines from being universally recommended to being for select high-risk groups and/or for patients who decide to take them based on consultation between patient and provider, New York State is adhering to

87 the vaccination schedule as it was previously structured. The current changes could place additional administrative burden on providers as shared clinical decision-making, that is decisions made after patient’s consultation with providers, may require documentation for billing purposes. Because VFC only covers the cost of vaccines that are recommended by the CDC, it's possible that future changes to the vaccination schedule could result in the cost of some vaccines being passed down from federal government to New York State or to the city. This is of particular concern for influenza, RSV, and rotavirus, three conditions among the diseases of interest for which children ages 14 and under account for a significant share of cases.
